result:
Neither number is the right starting point, because "more agents always give better results" isn't true.

Each extra agent adds costs:
- **Tokens.** Every agent carries its own instructions and context, and agents pass messages to each other. You pay for all of it on every request. Your budget is small, so this matters.
- **Handoff errors.** Information gets lost or garbled each time one agent passes work to another.
- **More to debug.** With ten agents, finding out which one went wrong is hard to do before a design review.

Think of a group project. Ten people on a one-page report spend more time coordinating than writing. Splitting only pays off when the work is big enough to share, and when the pieces really are separate.

For the makerspace assistant, take a request like "How do I set up the laser cutter, and book it Thursday at 3?" That is one short chain: look up the manual, check the calendar, make the booking. A single agent with three tools handles it. Part of it may not need an agent at all. If booking always follows the same steps, a fixed workflow is cheaper and more predictable.

Splitting starts to pay off in two cases:
1. One agent's context is overloaded, for example because it has too many tools or manuals to choose between.
2. Separate pieces of work can run at the same time, independently.

So I'd start with one agent and add a second only when you can name a specific problem the split fixes. Your team should be able to give that reason at the review.

Here's a question to check this landed. Suppose the manual-answering part keeps mixing up machines because its context is crammed with every manual. Would that be a reason to split, or a reason to fix something else first?

I can also teach a lesson on when multi-agent designs pay off, which is one of your mission goals.
